To fix (2)

To fix Exact P-Values

What we found

We found 2 imprecise p values out of 46 detected p values.

Show details

Reporting p values imprecisely (e.g., p < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in p value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., p = .032) unless p values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use p < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., “decreased at the p < .05 significance threshold”).

P-Value Text

ps > .37 Structural Inequality was no longer associated with unfairness (b = 0.26, 95% CI [-0.31, 0.83], p = .372), both indirect effects were nonsignificant (ps > .37), and its total effects were reduced and nonsignificant for both redistribution support (b = 0.28, p = .361) and distress (b = 0.57, p = .259…

Cells longer than 300 characters are cut (…).

The APA manual states: Report exact p values (e.g., p = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report p values less than .001 as p < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a p value meta-analysis), so report p values with three digits.

American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association.

To check (6)

To check Non-Significant P Value Check

What we found

We found 12 non-significant p values that should be checked for appropriate interpretation.

Show details

Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is ‘no effect’, ‘no difference’, or that groups are ‘the same’ after p > 0.05.

It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is ‘not significantly’ different, although this just restates that p > 0.05.

Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values.

For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see:

Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742.

Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167.

For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see Improving Your Statistical Inferences.

To check Codebook Check

What we found

We found no codebook or README documentation for the 28598 extracted data columns.

Show details

This module checks whether each extracted data column is documented in a codebook or README, and flags documented variables that never appear in the data.

We examined 1 codebook/README/label source and 28598 data columns across 35 files.

No codebook or README documentation was found, so no data columns could be matched to variable definitions.

Duplicated Column Names

  • Duplicated column names in study3b_raw.csv. 225 column names appear more than once (worst: inequality_1×177, inequality_2×177, inequality_3×177, lonely_1×177, lonely_2×177), so 10036 of the file’s 10797 columns share a name with another. This usually means a survey loop/merge exported repeated blocks without numbering each iteration; the repeats cannot be told apart and can only be documented once. Consider re-exporting with per-iteration column names.

  • Duplicated column names in study3a_raw.csv. 65 column names appear more than once (worst: Afraid×178, Amazed×178, Angry×178, Annoyed×178, anomie_1×178), so 11569 of the file’s 13240 columns share a name with another. This usually means a survey loop/merge exported repeated blocks without numbering each iteration; the repeats cannot be told apart and can only be documented once. Consider re-exporting with per-iteration column names.

The files metacheck lists below were not read from it — they were retrieved from the OSF registration’s own copy, which is separate from and unaffected by the project’s access setting. Code Comments

Best programming practice is to add comments to code, to explain what the code does (to yourself in the future, or peers who want to re-use your code). All your code files had comments.

Missing Files

All files loaded in the code were present in the repository.

Absolute Paths

Best programming practice is to use relative file paths (e.g., ‘./files’) instead of absolute file paths (e.g., ‘C://Lakens/project_dir/files’) as these folder names do not exist on other computers. No absolute file paths were found in any of the code files.

Working Directory (setwd)

Best programming practice is to avoid setwd() in analysis code: it hardcodes an assumption about the working directory (often an absolute path on the author’s own machine), so the code breaks when run anywhere else. Keep the working directory as the caller sets it and use relative paths. No setwd() calls were found in any of the code files.

Package Installation (install.packages)

Best programming practice is to avoid install.packages() in analysis code: it installs software on whoever runs the script without asking, which is at minimum disruptive (an unexpected install, network access, a package version the author never tested against) and at worst a security risk if it points at an untrusted repository. Document required packages instead (a README, or a list of them: an renv.lock/DESCRIPTION for R, a requirements.txt for Python). No install.packages() calls were found in any of the code files.

Libraries / Imports

Best programming practice is to load all required libraries/imports in one block near the top of the code. In 1 code file, libraries/imports were at multiple places (i.e., with more than 3 non-comment lines in between).

Packages / Dependencies

We ran automated data-quality checks on 28598 columns; 1571 columns have at least one potential issue (1432 columns with no observed values (entirely empty); 290 columns whose names become identical when special characters are removed; 18 columns of free text that may contain personal detail; 12 columns with leading/trailing whitespace; 6 columns with values in a legacy (non-UTF-8) encoding; 4 columns with numeric values stored as text). 75 survey respondents were flagged for possible careless responding (17 of them only via short-scale straightlining, which can be normal answering). We detected demographic columns for Age, Gender, Race. 4 files are a Qualtrics survey export (72 rows look like previews/unfinished responses to review). 1 of 1 spreadsheet file has at least one formatting issue (colour coding, merged cells, empty rows/columns, or an offset header).

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.

We examined 28598 columns across 35 data files.

Issues Identified

1572 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

About the personal-information flags. These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

  • Column names are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (email, telefoonnummer, geboortedatum, …). A column called phone_number flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
  • Values are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
  • Free text is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means look at this column. Where the data is already de-identified (an ip column reading Anonymized, a name column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

4 of the 35 data files are a Qualtrics survey export. Spreadsheet Formatting

We examined 1 spreadsheet file in the repository; 1 has at least one formatting issue.

File Sheet Issue Detail
Study3_Measures_Scoring_FINAL_with_item_wording.xlsx NA Not a rectangular dataset This file reads as a table but is not a usable dataset (86% of columns are free text, not variables). Store the data as a plain rectangular table (one header row, one column per variable) with a codebook.

Spreadsheet formatting such as colour, merged cells, and blank rows/columns is not preserved when data are read programmatically or exported to CSV. Store data as a plain rectangular table (one header row, one column per variable, no colour-encoded meaning) so it is machine-readable.

Careless Responding

75 distinct respondents were flagged for straightlining: giving the same answer for at least 80% of the items in a multi-item scale of 5 items or more. One respondent can be flagged in several scales; the table below is one row per person, and the Longest run column gives the run that triggered the strongest flag, so you can check it against the raw data.

Of these, 17 were flagged only by short-scale straightlining (a run of identical answers on a scale of 7 items or fewer). On a short, one-directional scale, answering consistently is often normal, coherent responding rather than carelessness — treat these as weak signals and inspect the actual responses before excluding anyone.

These are prompts to inspect those rows, not definitive judgements.

What this does not cover. Only 3 of 35 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

Execution

The code was run. Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 22 scripts: 4 ran without error, 16 errored, 1 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse, and 1 was run by another script with source(). Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions. 7 scripts stopped on a file another script writes, so they were run once more after the other scripts: 05_study2_cleaning.Rmd (situation_lookup.rds); 09_study3a_cleaning.Rmd (situation_lookup.rds); 06_study2_main.Rmd (study2_clean.rds); 07_study2_supplement.Rmd (study2_clean.rds); 08_study2_OSF.Rmd (study2_clean.rds); 10_study3a_supplement.Rmd (study3a_clean.rds); 11_study3a_OSF.Rmd (study3a_clean.rds). Which script must run first can be stated in a README, or shown by numbering the file names (01_, 02_). A script looked for 4 files in another folder than the deposit has them, so before running it once more we copied them there: raw/scenario_rating_structural_coder1.csv to raw/raw/scenario_rating_structural_coder1.csv for 14_study3b_supplement.Rmd; raw/scenario_rating_structural_coder2.csv to raw/raw/scenario_rating_structural_coder2.csv for 14_study3b_supplement.Rmd; raw/scenario_rating_lifestyle_coder1.csv to raw/raw/scenario_rating_lifestyle_coder1.csv for 14_study3b_supplement.Rmd; raw/scenario_rating_lifestyle_coder2.csv to raw/raw/scenario_rating_lifestyle_coder2.csv for 14_study3b_supplement.Rmd. Building paths from the top of the project (as with here::here()), or keeping the folders the code expects, solves this. A script wrote into a folder that the deposit does not have, so we made it and ran it once more: llm/scenario_prompts_cleaned_full for llm_prompts_study1_cleaned.Rmd. Keeping the (empty) output folders in the deposit, or making them in the code with dir.create(), solves this.

> definitions <- "
> You will read a short scenario describing economic inequality.
> 
> Rate the situation on two independent scales from 0 to 10.
> 
> ------------------------------------------------------------------
> 
> 1. Structural Inequality (0 = Not at all structural, 10 = Extremely structural)
> 
> Definition:
> Inequality that materialises through disparities in access to
> core life domains and essential institutions.
> 
> Structural inequality refers to inequality in fundamental areas
> that shape people’s security, opportunities, and living conditions.
> 
> Includes situations involving:
> - Housing or homelessness
> - Employment, wages, or working conditions
> - Education access or opportunities
> - Healthcare access
> - Essential goods (e.g., food, heating, basic needs)
> - Transport and infrastructure
> - Financial stability and economic security
> 
> Key idea:
> Is the inequality rooted in basic life systems or essential living conditions?
> 
> ------------------------------------------------------------------
> 
> 2. Lifestyle Inequality (0 = Not at all lifestyle, 10 = Extremely lifestyle)
> 
> Definition:
> Inequality based on differences in social participation,
> consumption, or quality-of-life experiences.
> 
> Includes situations involving:
> - Dining, social outings, or leisure activities
> - Holidays and travel
> - Clothing or visible consumption
> - Non-essential shopping
> - Social comparisons with peers or family
> - Cultural participation and lifestyle experiences
> 
> Key idea:
> Is the inequality about lifestyle, leisure, or visible social participation?
> 
> ------------------------------------------------------------------
> 
> Important:
> - Focus only on the situation described.
> - Ignore the person's emotions.
> - The scenario may reflect both types.
> - Rate each scale independently.
> 
> ------------------------------------------------------------------
> 
> Return ONLY the following format:
> 
> Structural Inequality: X
> Lifestyle Inequality: X
> 
> Where X is a whole number between 0 and 10.
> Do not include any explanation.
> "
> dir.create(output_folder, showWarnings = FALSE)
> writeLines("v2_domain_aligned", file.path(output_folder, "prompt_version.txt"))
> for (i in seq_len(nrow(data))) {

> cat("\n", exclusions$paragraph, "\n\n", sep = "")

We recruited a London based sample of N = 172 participants via Prolific, quota sampled by gender, income, and political orientation. After excluding 12 for survey completion below 50% and 5 for failing 2 or more repeated attention checks, the final analytic sample was N = 155. Among retained participants, a further 6 individual situation rating rounds were removed for a failed attention check.

> participant_means <- dat %>%
>   group_by(ResponseId, scenario_type) %>%
>   summarise(across(all_of(names(outcomes)), ~ mean(.x, na.rm = TRUE)), .groups = "drop")
> ttest_results <- bind_rows(lapply(names(outcomes), function(v) {
>   wide <- participant_means %>%
>     dplyr::select(ResponseId, scenario_type, all_of(v)) %>%
>     pivot_wider(names_from = scenario_type, values_from = all_of(v)) %>%
>     drop_na()
>   diffs <- wide$Structural - wide$Lifestyle
>   n     <- length(diffs)
>   tt    <- t.test(wide$Structural, wide$Lifestyle, paired = TRUE)
>   d     <- mean(diffs) / sd(diffs)
>   se_d  <- sqrt(1 / n + d^2 / (2 * n))
>   tibble(Outcome       = outcomes[[v]],
>          n_pairs       = n,
>          M_structural  = round(mean(wide$Structural), 2),
>          SD_structural = round(sd(wide$Structural),   2),
>          M_lifestyle   = round(mean(wide$Lifestyle),  2),
>          SD_lifestyle  = round(sd(wide$Lifestyle),    2),
>          t             = round(unname(tt$statistic),  2),
>          df            = unname(tt$parameter),
>          p             = fmt_p(tt$p.value),
>          d             = round(d, 2),
>          d_CI_low      = round(d - 1.96 * se_d, 2),
>          d_CI_high     = round(d + 1.96 * se_d, 2))
> }))
> ft_tt <- style_ft(ttest_results,
>   caption = "Paired comparisons of Structural and Lifestyle situations, participant means (Study 2)")

> variance_partition <- bind_rows(lapply(names(outcomes), function(v) {
>   m_full <- lmer(as.formula(paste(v, "~ 1 + (1 | ResponseId) + (1 | Scenario_ID)")),
>                  data = dat, REML = FALSE)
>   m_part <- lmer(as.formula(paste(v, "~ 1 + (1 | ResponseId)")),
>                  data = dat, REML = FALSE)
>   vc    <- as.data.frame(VarCorr(m_full))
>   v_sit <- vc$vcov[vc$grp == "Scenario_ID"]
>   v_par <- vc$vcov[vc$grp == "ResponseId"]
>   v_res <- vc$vcov[vc$grp == "Residual"]
>   total <- v_sit + v_par + v_res
>   lrt   <- anova(m_part, m_full)
>   tibble(Outcome         = outcomes[[v]],
>          ICC_situation   = round(v_sit / total, 3),
>          ICC_participant = round(v_par / total, 3),
>          chisq           = round(lrt$Chisq[2], 2),
>          df              = lrt$Df[2],
>          p               = as.numeric(lrt$`Pr(>Chisq)`[2]))
> })) %>% mutate(p = fmt_p(as.numeric(p)))

> label_pattern <- paste0(
>   "^(Housing|Work|Dining_social_outing|Travel|Health|Homelessness|Education_qual|",
>   "Essential_shopping|Non_essential_shopping|Peer_comparison|Other_lifestyle|",
>   "Work_social|Other_living_cond_new)_\\d+$"
> )
> placeholders <- names(raw3a)[grepl(label_pattern, names(raw3a))]
> get_shown <- function(row, blocks) {
>   for (b in blocks) {
>     idx <- which(names(row) == b)
>     if (length(idx) == 0 || idx + 20 > length(row)) next
>     nearby <- names(row)[(idx + 1):min(length(row), idx + 20)]
>     if (any(!is.na(row[nearby]))) return(b)
>   }
>   NA_character_
> }
> raw3a$qualtrics_label <- apply(raw3a, 1, get_shown, blocks = placeholders)
> write_csv(
>   tibble(label = sort(unique(na.omit(raw3a$qualtrics_label)))),
>   file.path(DER, "study3a_labels.csv")
> )

We recruited a London based sample of N = 554 participants via Prolific, quota sampled by gender, income, and political orientation (data collected 25 Apr 2025 to 27 May 2025). After excluding 5 duplicate responses, 47 for no situation assignment and a further 10 for failing the attention check, the final analytic sample was N = 492.

> RAW <- "raw"
> DER <- "derived"
> OUT <- "Tables_Figures"
> FULL_RUN  <- "study1_llm_ratings.csv"
> REF_FILE  <- "scenario_id_reference_full_data_set.csv"
> OLD_RUN   <- "llm_ratings_adopted_run.csv"
> MATCH_TOL <- 0.2
> lookup <- readRDS(file.path(DER, "situation_lookup.rds")) %>%
>   mutate(Scenario_ID = as.character(Scenario_ID),
>          alias_of    = as.character(alias_of))
> full <- read_csv(file.path(RAW, FULL_RUN), show_col_types = FALSE) %>%
>   transmute(ref_id     = trimws(as.character(scenario_id)),
>             structural = as.numeric(Structural_rating),
>             lifestyle  = as.numeric(Lifestyle_rating))
> ref <- read_csv(file.path(RAW, REF_FILE), show_col_types = FALSE,
>                 locale = locale(encoding = "latin1")) %>%
>   transmute(ref_id = trimws(as.character(scenario_id)), ref_text = what_happened)
> stopifnot(!any(duplicated(full$ref_id)), !any(duplicated(ref$ref_id)))
> scored <- full %>% inner_join(ref, by = "ref_id")
> to_link <- lookup %>% filter(!(is_alias %in% TRUE))
> dm <- stringdist::stringdistmatrix(clean_match_text(scored$ref_text),
>                                    clean_match_text(to_link$what_happened),
>                                    method = "jw")
> best_idx  <- apply(dm, 2, which.min)
> best_dist <- apply(dm, 2, min)
> linked <- to_link %>%
>   transmute(Scenario_ID,
>             ref_id         = if_else(best_dist <= MATCH_TOL, scored$ref_id[best_idx], NA_character_),
>             match_distance = round(best_dist, 4)) %>%
>   left_join(scored %>% select(ref_id, structural, lifestyle), by = "ref_id")
> aliases <- lookup %>%
>   filter(is_alias %in% TRUE) %>%
>   select(Scenario_ID, alias_of) %>%
>   left_join(linked %>% select(alias_of = Scenario_ID, ref_id, match_distance,
>                               structural, lifestyle), by = "alias_of") %>%
>   select(-alias_of)
> scores <- bind_rows(linked, aliases) %>% arrange(Scenario_ID)
> cat("Stimulus pool situations:      ", nrow(scores), "\n",
>     "  of which aliases:            ", nrow(aliases), "\n",
>     "Linked to full run scores:     ", sum(!is.na(scores$structural)), "\n",
>     "Without scores:                ", sum(is.na(scores$structural)), "\n", sep = "")

> score_75 <- function(...) {
>   x <- cbind(...)
>   n_required <- ceiling(ncol(x) * .75)
>   out <- rowMeans(x, na.rm = TRUE)
>   out[rowSums(!is.na(x)) < n_required] <- NA_real_
>   out
> }
> std_beta_term <- function(model, term) {
>   mm <- model.matrix(model)
>   mf <- model.frame(model)
>   y <- model.response(mf)
> 
>   if (!term %in% colnames(mm)) {
>     return(NA_real_)
>   }
> 
>   b <- coef(model)[term]
>   sx <- sd(mm[, term], na.rm = TRUE)
>   sy <- sd(y, na.rm = TRUE)
> 
>   if (
>     length(b) == 0 ||
>     !is.finite(b) ||
>     !is.finite(sx) ||
>     !is.finite(sy) ||
>     sx == 0 ||
>     sy == 0
>   ) {
>     return(NA_real_)
>   }
> 
>   as.numeric(b * sx / sy)
> }

More detail

Ethics Approval Check

The paper appears to report data that the authors collected from people or animals, and it has an ethics statement.

We based this on:

All studies were approved by the XXX Research Ethics Committee and conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki, and all participants gave informed consent before taking part.

We recruited a London based sample of N = 476 participants via Prolific, quota sampled by gender, income, and political orientation.

Participants were aged 19 to 74 years (M = 39.23, SD = 12.35), and 46.5% identified as female.

Ethics statement:

All studies were approved by the XXX Research Ethics Committee and conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki, and all participants gave informed consent before taking part.

All studies were approved by the University of Sussex Sciences & Technology Cross-Schools Research Ethics Committee (Study 1: ER/CM989/1; Study 2: ER/CM989/3; Study 3a: ER/CM989/5; Study 3b: ER/CM989/6

Power Analysis Check

No power analyses were detected.

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen’s d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.
