Discussion Study 1 identified two broad forms of inequality encounter: (1) Structural Inequality and (2) Lifestyle Inequality. Structural Inequality encounters were reported more frequently and appraised as more unequal, unfair, and vivid, though dining and social outings was the single most common encounter category (18.2%). The two forms of encounter also differed in comparison type: Lifestyle Inequality encounters were predominantly upward whereas

Structural Inequality encounters were more varied. This is consistent with evidence that social comparisons under economic inequality tend to be upward in nature (Payne et al., 2017). The form of encounter described was largely consistent across demographic groups.

Study 2 addresses whether these appraisal differences reflect the encounters themselves or the individuals who reported them.

Study 2: Psychological Responses to Structural and Lifestyle Inequality Situations

Among Independent Observers

Study 1 showed that people reported two distinct forms of inequality encounter with differing appraisals, but those appraisals came from the same people who had lived them.

Study 2 therefore presented a random subset of the written situation descriptions generated in Study 1 to a new sample, testing whether the two forms were associated with different appraisals and political responses among naïve raters. We also strengthened measurement, replacing the single item inequality and unfairness measures with validated multiple item subscales and adding a measure of support for redistribution. We hypothesised that Structural Inequality situations would be rated as more unequal, more unfair, and more deserving of redistribution than Lifestyle Inequality situations.

Method

Participants. We recruited a London based sample of N = 172 participants, quota sampled by gender, income, and political orientation. After excluding 12 participants for survey completion below 50% and a further 5 for failing two or more repeated attention checks, the final analytic sample was N = 155. Participants were aged 20 to 75 years (M = 39.39, SD = 10.76), and 43.2% identified as female. Full demographic characteristics are reported in Table 1.

Design and Procedure.

From the written descriptions generated in Study 1, 178 were selected as experimental stimuli for the subsequent studies. Because situations varied considerably in length (Mdn = 68 words, range = 8 to 223), we selected situations of between 51 and 149 words to keep reading burden comparable across stimuli. Within each category identified in the content analysis, up to 15 situations were sampled at random, ensuring that all categories were represented rather than only the most frequently reported ones. This yielded 178 stimuli of relatively even length (Mdn = 79 words, range = 51 to 149). We employed a within subjects design in which participants were presented with seven situations drawn at random from this pool. Because the attention check was repeated for each situation, isolated failures were handled at the observation level, and six individual situation ratings were removed from otherwise retained participants. The final analytic dataset comprised 1,002 situation ratings.

Measures.

Perceived inequality and unfairness. Participants rated six items adapted from the Perceived Economic Inequality Scale (PEIS; Valtorta et al., 2024) on a 5 point scale (1 = Strongly disagree,5 = Strongly agree; e.g., "There is a lot of economic inequality in this situation" [inequality]; "The gap between those better off and worse off is fair in this situation" [unfairness, reverse scored]). Internal consistency was high for both subscales (ω = .87, .86; see Table S10b).

Support for redistribution.

Participants rated two items adapted from García-Castro and colleagues (2020) on the same 5-point scale as above (e.g., "Based on this situation, I am motivated to support plans to redistribute wealth"). The composite showed excellent reliability (α = .96, r = .93).

Vividness.

Participants rated each situation's vividness with a single item rated on a 5 point scale (1 = Not at all vivid,5 = Extremely vivid).

Analytic plan.

Paired t tests on participant level means were conducted first to provide simple effect size estimates for each outcome. Cross classified linear mixed effects models were then fitted for each outcome with situation form (0 = Lifestyle Inequality,1 = Structural Inequality) as the predictor, controlling for vividness, and including random intercepts for both participants and situations to account for the crossed data structure, in which each participant rated multiple situations and each situation was rated by multiple participants. Robustness checks adding demographic covariates are reported in Table S13.

The preregistered repeated measures ANCOVA is reported in Table P3, and this departure from the preregistered plan is listed in Table P1.

Results

Simple comparisons.

Paired t tests aggregating ratings to the participant level showed that Structural compared to Lifestyle Inequality situations were rated as significantly more unequal (M = 3.92, SD = 0.55 vs. M = 3.45, SD = 0.70), t(154) = 7.68, p < .001, d = 0.62, 95% CI [0.45, 0.79], more unfair (M = 3.67, SD = 0.67 vs. M = 3.00, SD = 0.78), t(154) = 11.44, p < .001, d = 0.92, 95% CI [0.73, 1.11], and were associated with stronger redistribution support (M = 3.61, SD = 0.95 vs. M = 2.95, SD = 1.11), t(154) = 9.84, p < .001, d = 0.79, 95% CI [0.61, 0.97]. Effect sizes were medium to large across all outcomes.

Mixed effects models.

Variance partitioning confirmed substantial clustering at both the situation and participant level across all outcomes; ICCs were .28 (situation) and .12 (participant) for perceived inequality, .24 (situation) and .27 (participant) for unfairness, and .15 (situation) and .46 (participant) for redistribution support (Table S15). Model fit comparisons confirmed that adding situation level random intercepts significantly improved fit over participant only models for perceived inequality (χ²(1) = 144.04, p < .001), perceived unfairness (χ²(1) = 142.37, p < .001), and redistribution support (χ²(1) = 99.65, p < .001), confirming that the cross classified structure was warranted across all outcomes.

Multicollinearity checks indicated no concerns across all models (VIFs < 1.01). Vividness was positively associated with all outcomes (ps < .001). Situation form and vividness explained a modest share of variance across outcomes (marginal R² = .14, .15, .11 for perceived inequality, unfairness, and redistribution support), rising substantially once participant and situation clustering was included (conditional R² = .47, .53, .63).

Results were robust to the inclusion of demographic covariates, with the effect of situation form remaining significant for perceived inequality, unfairness, and redistribution support. Among the covariates, older age was associated with lower perceived unfairness, while political orientation was associated with perceived unfairness and redistribution support but not perceived inequality. Given these associations, we additionally explored whether political orientation moderated the effect of situation form. No significant situation form × political orientation interactions were observed for any outcome (see Tables S13 and S14).

Interactions between situation form and each demographic characteristic, tested as preregistered (H2), are reported in Table P4.

Discussion

Study 2 showed that Structural Inequality situations were associated with higher perceived inequality, unfairness, and redistribution support than Lifestyle Inequality situations when rated by independent observers with no personal connection to the original events. This suggests that the differences identified in Study 1 are not solely attributable to the individuals who originally reported the encounters but are also systematically related to characteristics of the situations themselves.

Studies 3a and 3b: Political and Psychological Responses to Structural and Lifestyle

Inequality

Studies 1 and 2 showed that people encounter economic inequality in two recurring forms and that these forms are appraised differently and are associated with different levels of support for redistribution. In Studies 3a and 3b we asked why. We reasoned that the two forms differ in which feature of inequality they make salient, and that this difference matters for the psychological response. Structural Inequality situations, involving access to essential goods and institutions, foreground differences in what people have (i.e., housing, education and resources), which we suggest makes unfairness a particularly relevant appraisal. Past research shows that people are troubled less by inequality itself than by inequality judged to have been unfairly produced (Lerner, 1980; Starmans et al., 2017). Allocations judged unfair often invite correction, consistent with evidence that justice based concerns, rather than perceived inequality alone, are associated with support for redistribution (Petkanopoulou et al., 2025). Lifestyle Inequality, by contrast, was appraised as less unfair in Studies 1 and 2 and was associated with weaker support for redistribution. We therefore expected Structural Inequality, but not Lifestyle Inequality, to be associated with greater support for redistribution because it was more likely to be appraised as unfair.

Lifestyle Inequality situations, involving consumption, leisure, and social participation, foreground differences in what people can do (i.e., routines, choice and taste), which we suggest makes social comparison a particularly relevant process. Study 1 found that Lifestyle Inequality encounters were characterised almost exclusively by upward comparisons, and Social Comparison Theory has long held that upward comparison can produce negative affect and lower wellbeing (Collins, 1996; Festinger, 1954). There is also longitudinal evidence, from a sample of college students, linking perceived inequality to poorer wellbeing via upward comparison (Du et al., 2024). We therefore expected Lifestyle Inequality to be associated with greater psychological distress because it was more likely to involve upward comparison. Unfairness appraisal and upward social comparison were thus specified as two distinct processes through which the two forms of inequality could be associated with different psychological consequences.

Both predictions concern the form of inequality a situation contains rather than how much inequality it appears to involve. This distinction matters because existing research largely treats perceived inequality as a quantity that people estimate, with effects expected to scale with perceived magnitude (Jachimowicz et al., 2023; Willis et al., 2022). Inequality form and perceived magnitude are difficult to separate in practice, however, because Structural Inequality situations were also rated as more unequal in Study 2. Therefore, in both studies we entered perceived inequality as an additional control in our analyses, allowing us to test whether the form of inequality was associated with unfairness and social comparison independently of how unequal a situation was perceived to be.

Studies 3a and 3b also changed how the two forms were measured. Treating them as mutually exclusive in Studies 1 and 2 implied that Lifestyle Inequality occurred in the absence of Structural Inequality. Most situations, however, combine both to varying degrees.

For example, a visit to a friend with a much larger home may render housing, and thus the distribution of resources, salient, while at the same time evoking upward comparison and raising questions about one's own position in society. A binary classification therefore treats a situation that combines both forms as wholly one or the other, which introduces measurement error and risks attributing a situation's associations to whichever feature dominated its coding.

Both studies therefore scored each situation continuously on both dimensions and entered them simultaneously in our statistical analyses, so that each could be estimated while holding the other constant.

Method

Study 3a was designed and preregistered before we updated the coding scheme, using the binary classification of situation form established in Studies 1 and 2. Because a binary label treats a situation that combines both forms as wholly one or the other, the continuous scores described below were subsequently developed for Study 3b to accommodate situations containing characteristics of both Structural and Lifestyle Inequality. Because the two studies used the same design, situation pool, and measures, differing only in the response scales used by participants (5 point scales in Study 3a and 7 point scales in Study 3b), we applied the continuous scores retrospectively to Study 3a. This allowed us to analyse both datasets using a consistent operationalisation of situation form, increasing the available sample size and precision of the estimates. In Studies 1 and 2, the continuous scores corresponded closely with the original binary classification, and their associations with perceived inequality and unfairness were consistent with the binary results (Tables S29 and S32). The pooled analyses were not preregistered and are therefore exploratory. The preregistered analyses for both studies are reported in the Supplementary Materials (Tables P6 to P10), and departures from the preregistered plans are listed in Table P1.

Participants. Both samples were recruited in London via Prolific and quota sampled by gender, income, and political orientation. Participants who had taken part in Study 3a were excluded from Study 3b, so the two samples were independent. In Study 3a, we recruited N = 554 participants. After excluding 5 duplicate responses, 47 with no situation assignment, and a further 10 for failing the attention check, the final analytic sample was N = 492. Participants were aged 20 to 74 years (M = 38.82, SD = 12.02), and 55.1% identified as female. In Study 3b, we recruited N = 504 participants. After excluding 41 duplicate responses, 9 for missing key identifiers, and a further 12 for failing the attention check, the final analytic sample was N = 442. Participants were aged 18 to 80 years (M = 40.76, SD = 12.77), and 49.5% identified as female. The combined analytic sample comprised 934 participants. Full demographic characteristics are reported in Table 1.

Design and Procedure.

Both studies employed a between subjects design in which each participant rated one randomly assigned situation from the 178 situation pool described in Study 2. Across the two analytic samples, all 178 situations received at least one rating, and 172 were rated in both studies. After providing consent and demographic information, participants rated the situation on perceived inequality, unfairness, redistribution support, psychological distress, and vividness. The studies differed in response format, with 5 point scales in Study 3a and 7 point scales in Study 3b. To ensure comparability across studies, all measures were converted to percent of maximum possible (POMP) scores ranging from 0 to 100 (Cohen et al., 1999). Because POMP scores rescale each response format by a fixed amount determined by the scale itself, independent of each sample's variability, both studies share a common metric on which coefficients represent change on a 0 to 100 scale. The key paths did not differ between the studies when each was estimated separately (Table S28).

Situation Characterisation.

Each situation rated in Studies 3a and 3b was scored on the Structural and Lifestyle Inequality dimensions established in Study 1 using the open weight large language model Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3. Rather than generating text, the model was prompted to act as a rater, assigning each situation a score from 0 to 10 on each dimension independently. Mistral was selected over proprietary alternatives such as GPT-4 because its weights are permanently available and fixed, making the scoring procedure reproducible despite potential updates to proprietary models (Abdurahman et al., 2025; Bunt et al., 2025). The final zero shot prompt provided the construct definitions and qualifying subcategories but no example ratings.

Two human coders independently rated the same situations on both dimensions without access to the LLM generated scores. Agreement between the human coders was good (Structural Inequality ICC = .768; Lifestyle Inequality ICC = .734). Their ratings provided a benchmark for refining the LLM prompt and evaluating the resulting scores. The final prompt is shown in Table 4, with full prompt development details reported in Table S20.

Table 4.

LLM Rating Prompt Used to Characterise Structural and Lifestyle Inequality (Study 3b)

Section Content Task You will read a short scenario describing economic inequality. Rate the situation on two independent scales from 0 to 10.

Structural

Inequality (0 = Not at all structural,10 = Extremely structural)

Inequality that materialises through disparities in access to core life domains and essential institutions, referring to inequality in fundamental areas that shape people's security, opportunities, and living conditions. Includes housing or homelessness; employment, wages, or working conditions; education access; healthcare access; essential goods (e.g., food, heating, basic needs); transport and infrastructure; financial stability and economic security. Key idea: is the inequality rooted in basic life systems or essential living conditions?

Lifestyle Inequality (0 = Not at all lifestyle,10 = Extremely lifestyle) Inequality based on differences in social participation, consumption, or quality of life experiences. Includes dining, social outings, or leisure activities; holidays and travel; clothing or visible consumption; nonessential shopping; social comparisons with peers or family; cultural participation and lifestyle experiences. Key idea: is the inequality about lifestyle, leisure, or visible social participation?

Instructions Focus only on the situation described. Ignore the person's emotions. The scenario may reflect both types. Rate each scale independently.

Output format Structural Inequality: X / Lifestyle Inequality: X, where X is a whole number between 0 and 10. No explanation returned.

Agreement between the final LLM scores and mean human ratings was acceptable for Structural Inequality (ICC = .625, r = .63) and good for Lifestyle Inequality (ICC = .790, r = .80). The two LLM derived dimensions were moderately negatively correlated across situations (r = -.58), indicating that situations characterised by greater Structural Inequality tended to contain fewer Lifestyle Inequality characteristics. These model scores were used as the continuous predictors in subsequent analyses (Table S21). The distribution of situations across the two dimensions is shown in Table S22 and Figure S6.

Measures.

Perceived inequality, unfairness, and redistribution support.

Participants rated perceived inequality, unfairness, and redistribution support using the same items as Study 2, on 5 point (Study 3a) or 7 point (Study 3b) scales. Internal consistency was good in both studies for perceived inequality (ω = .85 and .86), perceived unfairness (ω = .84 and .87), and redistribution support (α = .88 and .93; Tables S16b and S18b).

The reverse scored unfairness item loaded comparatively weakly in Study 3a (λ = .62), and results were unchanged when it was omitted (Table S27). comparison direction (0 = downward,1 = upward), restricted to situations with a clear comparison direction. All three models were re-estimated with perceived inequality included as an additional covariate. Indirect effects were evaluated using MLR based standard errors and 95% confidence intervals. To assess whether pooling obscured differences between studies, each model was also fitted as a two group model, allowing the key paths to vary between Studies 3a and 3b. These paths were then compared using Wald tests.

Results

Intercorrelations among key study variables are presented in Table 5. Lifestyle Inequality was positively associated with upward social comparison and negatively associated with perceived unfairness, whereas Structural Inequality showed the opposite pattern. Redistribution support and psychological distress were positively correlated.

Mediation models.

Figure 3 presents path coefficients from three primary mediation models testing the appraisal pathway to redistribution support and psychological distress, respectively, and the comparison pathway to psychological distress, with Structural and Lifestyle Inequality entered as simultaneous predictors in all models. Full path coefficients and indirect effects are reported in Tables S24a and S24b. Results were robust to the inclusion of demographic covariates (Table S26) and to omitting the weakly loading unfairness item (Table S27).

Replication across studies.

Discussion

Studies 3a and 3b examined two established psychological processes: unfairness appraisal, which was associated with redistribution support and distress, and upward social comparison, which was associated with distress. Situations scoring higher on Structural Inequality were rated as more unfair, so the same appraisal pathway carried both political and psychological responses. Lifestyle Inequality operated through both processes, but with opposite consequences for distress. Because these situations were rated as less unfair, the appraisal route carried both weaker redistribution support and lower distress. Because they were more likely to involve upward comparison, the comparison route carried greater distress. The two routes therefore pulled distress in opposite directions, and on balance situations higher in Lifestyle Inequality were associated with lower distress.

These psychological processes also differed in their dependence on perceived inequality. After controlling for perceived inequality, the Structural Inequality appraisal pathway was no longer statistically significant, whereas the Lifestyle Inequality comparison pathway remained significant. This suggests that the association between Lifestyle Inequality and distress through upward comparison is not explained by differences in perceived inequality magnitude. One finding ran counter to expectation: in both sets of models, Lifestyle Inequality was negatively associated with distress once comparison was held constant. This pattern suggests that Lifestyle Inequality may be associated with distress particularly when it prompts unfavourable upward comparison, rather than being intrinsically distressing.

General Discussion

Across four studies, we identified two forms in which people encounter economic inequality in everyday life: Structural Inequality, involving disparities in access to essential goods and institutions such as housing, employment, education, and healthcare, and Lifestyle Inequality, involving differences in consumption, leisure, and social participation. These forms were associated with political and psychological responses through partly distinct processes. Structural Inequality was associated with redistribution support and distress through unfairness appraisals that tracked how unequal a situation appeared, whereas Lifestyle Inequality was associated with distress through upward social comparison, independently of perceived inequality. This research makes three contributions. First, it identifies forms of inequality from the encounters people report rather than from domains specified in advance. Second, by presenting these encounters to independent raters, it shows that the forms reflect characteristics of the situations rather than only of the people who reported them. Third, by examining political and psychological responses together, it shows that the two forms relate to these responses through partly distinct processes, and that the comparison route holds independently of how unequal a situation appears. Together, these findings suggest that the consequences of inequality depend not only on how much inequality people perceive but also on how they encounter it.

Two findings support the second contribution. In Study 1, the reported inequality encounter was largely unrelated to participants' income, status, education, or political orientation. When independent samples rated the same situations in Studies 2, 3a, and 3b, they consistently judged Structural Inequality as more unequal and more unfair than Lifestyle Inequality.

Unfairness appraisal was related to both forms, in opposite directions. For Structural Inequality, stronger unfairness appraisals were associated with both greater support for redistribution and more psychological distress. Each association has a counterpart in existing work. Perceived inequality has been associated with psychological distress (Du et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2026). On the political side, objections to inequality have been shown to track unfairness rather than the size of the gap (Starmans et al., 2017), and justice based concerns have been associated with redistribution support and collective action intentions (Petkanopoulou et al., 2025). Drawing attention to structural sources or domains of inequality has likewise been associated with stronger support for redistribution and other action to reduce inequality (Dolifka et al., 2025; Klebl & Jetten, 2023; Soler-Martínez et al., 2025).

Previous research has demonstrated that people perceive economic inequality through everyday differences in consumption, leisure, and access to opportunities, and that these representations are associated with inequality awareness and, in some analyses, redistribution preferences (García-Castro, García-Sánchez, Montoya-Lozano, et al., 2022). The present research extends this work by examining specific encounters rather than general differences between friends, by separating characteristics of the reported situations from those of the individuals who experienced them, and by testing how these characteristics relate to political and psychological responses through unfairness appraisal and social comparison. At the level of individual encounters, perceived unfairness was associated with both redistribution support and psychological distress. The two responses were not equally situational, however.

Redistribution support varied more between participants than between situations, whereas psychological distress varied more with the situation encountered.

Turning to the role of perceived inequality magnitude, once perceived inequality was controlled, Structural Inequality was no longer associated with unfairness, and its indirect associations with redistribution support and distress were no longer significant. Situations involving housing, employment, education, or healthcare were appraised as unfair largely because the gaps they involve were seen as large. It may be that a gap in these domains must be large before they are seen as a failure of fair distribution of the kind that violates expectations about just outcomes (Lerner, 1980), though this was not tested here. For Structural Inequality, these findings are therefore broadly consistent with accounts emphasising the perceived magnitude of economic disparities.

Lifestyle Inequality showed a different pattern of associations. While these situations were rated as less unequal and less unfair, greater Lifestyle Inequality was associated with more upward social comparison, which in turn was associated with greater psychological distress. This is consistent with long standing evidence that comparison with better off others is associated with negative self-evaluation (Collins, 1996; Festinger, 1954). This pattern is also consistent with work linking perceived inequality to lower wellbeing through comparative processes (Du et al., 2024; Melita et al., 2025). Du and colleagues (2024) found that people who perceived more inequality in society reported lower wellbeing a year later, partly through more upward comparison. The present findings extend this work by showing that, at the level of individual encounters, the comparison pathway was specifically associated with Lifestyle Inequality characteristics rather than Structural Inequality characteristics. Moreover, this association remained significant after controlling for perceived inequality, which was itself unrelated to comparison direction. Upward comparison may therefore be more closely associated with the content of an inequality encounter than with its perceived magnitude. Importantly, whereas Du and colleagues (2024) measured individuals' general tendency to make upward socioeconomic comparisons, the present research shows that the upward comparison represented within a single encounter is associated with observers' psychological distress.

One further result is notable. Lifestyle Inequality was positively associated with distress through upward social comparison but negatively associated with distress once comparison was held constant. The negative association was larger, such that situations higher in Lifestyle Inequality were associated with lower distress overall. This pattern suggests that the psychological implications of Lifestyle Inequality may depend on the characteristics of the encounter. Although situations higher in Lifestyle Inequality were more likely to involve upward comparisons, which were associated with greater distress, other characteristics of these situations may be associated with lower distress. One possibility is that Lifestyle Inequality encounters, often involving consumption, leisure, and social participation, are less threatening than disparities involving essential resources and opportunities. Alternatively, some may involve opportunities for social contact, which has been associated with greater wellbeing (Sandstrom & Dunn, 2014). These explanations remain speculative, however, as the characteristics underlying the negative association were not directly examined.

These patterns point to a gap between how inequality is typically defined and measured in research and how people encounter and evaluate it in their everyday lives. The dominant approach to measuring subjective inequality asks how large a disparity is perceived to be (Jachimowicz et al., 2023; Phillips et al., 2025), and the case for studying perception rather than objective indices has been made on the basis of such measures (Schmalor & Heine, 2022; Valtorta et al., 2024). We adapted these items to refer to a specific situation rather than to society in general. For Structural Inequality, the present findings were broadly consistent with this approach: its associations with unfairness, redistribution support, and distress were closely tied to how unequal the situations were rated to be. However, Lifestyle Inequality revealed two important limitations of focusing on magnitude alone. First, situations higher in Lifestyle Inequality were associated with lower perceived unfairness, even after controlling for perceived inequality. This suggests that recognising economic differences does not necessarily mean appraising them as unfair, with implications for understanding why perceived inequality may not always translate into support for redistribution. Second, Lifestyle Inequality was associated with psychological distress through upward comparison, independently of perceived inequality magnitude. A measure asking how unequal a situation appears would therefore register these situations weakly, while the distress associated with them would remain unaccounted for. Together, these findings suggest that understanding the political and psychological consequences of inequality requires attention not only to the magnitude of disparities people perceive, but also to the content of the encounters through which inequality becomes apparent.

Examining these associations more precisely involved treating Structural and Lifestyle Inequality as continuous rather than mutually exclusive dimensions. Doing so allowed both forms to be represented within the same situation and their associations to be estimated simultaneously. When the same scores were applied to all four studies, the associations with unfairness followed the same pattern in each (Table S32). Agreement between model-based scores and trained human coders suggests that the recovered LLM scores tracked human judgement reasonably closely. We think that this illustrates how language model characterisation can offer a workable route to studying open ended accounts at a scale that manual coding cannot reach. This is in line with emerging evaluations of these models for social science use (Abdurahman et al., 2025). Applied elsewhere, the same approach could be used to characterise other kinds of reported experience along theoretically specified dimensions, where the relevant distinctions are known but the volume of text makes hand coding impractical.

Several limitations should be noted. Situations were randomly assigned to raters, but their structural and lifestyle content was measured rather than manipulated, and the mediators were assessed alongside the outcomes, so the analyses describe associations rather than causal sequences and require confirmatory testing. The pooled mediation models for Studies 3a and 3b also departed from the preregistered plans and should be treated as exploratory. In addition, the continuous scores agreed less closely with human coders for Structural than for Lifestyle Inequality (ICC = .625 against .790), suggesting greater uncertainty in the characterisation of Structural Inequality. The situations were also recalled rather than encountered in the moment, and in Studies 2, 3a, and 3b they were rated from written descriptions rather than by the people who experienced them, so the ratings reflect how observers interpreted the accounts. Finally, this situation level design had less purchase on political attitudes than on psychological responses, with redistribution support varying more between participants than between situations. Redistribution was also measured as a single composite that may obscure differences between taxing the wealthy and assisting those in need, and separating the two components would allow these to be examined more closely.

Conclusion

The inequality situations people encounter in everyday life cannot be fully understood by only asking how unequal they appear. We found that distinct forms of inequality, Structural and Lifestyle Inequality, are associated with different political and psychological responses through unfairness appraisals and upward social comparisons. Understanding economic inequality therefore requires attention not only to its perceived magnitude but also to how inequality is encountered in everyday life.

Psychological distress. Participants rated four items adapted to a situational response context from the Patient Health Questionnaire 4 (PHQ 4; Kroenke et al., 2009) on 5 point (Study 3a) or 7 point (Study 3b) Likert scales (1 = Strongly disagree, 5 or7 = Strongly agree). Items related to anxiety (GAD 2) included "In this situation I would feel nervous, anxious or on edge," and items related to depression (PHQ 2) included "In this situation I would feel down, depressed or hopeless." Internal consistency was very high in both studies (ω = .91 and .93). Social comparison direction. Comparison direction for each situation was drawn from the coding established in Study 1, in which three independent raters classified situations as involving an upward comparison, downward comparison, both directions, or no explicit comparison. Situations classified as both or no comparison were excluded, yielding 741 ratings with a clear comparison direction across 140 situations, comprising 517 upward and 224 downward comparisons. Vividness. Participants rated the vividness of the situation using a single item on a 5 point (Study 3a) or 7 point (Study 3b) Likert scale (1 = Not at all vivid, 5 or7 = Extremely vivid). Analytic plan. Analyses were conducted in R using the lavaan package on the pooled data from both studies, with a study indicator (0 = Study 3a,1 = Study 3b) entered as a covariate in every model. Because multiple participants evaluated the same situations within and across studies, responses were clustered by situation, and the MLR estimator with cluster robust standard errors was used to account for nonindependence (ICCs = 17.6% for perceived unfairness, 5.8% for redistribution support, and 29.5% for psychological distress). All continuous predictors were mean centred prior to analysis. We tested three mediation models, entering Structural and Lifestyle Inequality as simultaneous predictors and controlling for vividness and study throughout. Perceived inequality was strongly associated with unfairness (b = 0.65, 95% CI [0.59, 0.71], p < .001), and the Structural Inequality appraisal pathway was no longer statistically significant after controlling for perceived inequality. Structural Inequality was no longer associated with unfairness (b = 0.26, 95% CI [-0.31, 0.83], p = .372), both indirect effects were nonsignificant (ps > .37), and its total effects were reduced and nonsignificant for both redistribution support (b = 0.28, p = .361) and distress (b = 0.57, p = .259). The Lifestyle Inequality comparison pathway was largely unchanged. Lifestyle Inequality remained associated with upward comparison (b = 0.054, 95% CI [0.026, 0.082], p < .001), which remained associated with distress (b = 18.77, 95% CI [12.79, 24.75], p < .001), yielding a significant indirect effect (b = 1.01, 95% CI [0.39, 1.63], p = .001). Perceived inequality was not associated with comparison direction (p = .158). The negative direct association of Lifestyle Inequality with distress also held (b = -2.29, 95% CI [-3.28, -1.30], p < .001), as did its negative total effect (b = -1.28, 95% CI [-2.45, -0.10], p = .033). Lifestyle Inequality also remained associated with lower unfairness (b = -1.36, 95% CI [-1.87, -0.84], p < .001), with significant negative indirect effects on both outcomes (ps < .001).
